dart2js compile time vs. generated code shape

2026-10-02T06:59:23.708763 · Dart 3.14.0-edge.25a38e4d0d2a222e4a17311809527a03481f1b41 · macos Version 27.0.1 (Build 26A434) · 10 cores · 259 compiles, N = 1 to 4000

Each point is a single dart compile js -O3 --csp of a generated program with N classes, all instantiated in one main. Variants change one aspect of the generated code; see variants in gen.dart.

Comparing variants: Synthetic ZBase_i classes

Each ZBase_i has an int field plus some combination of ==, hashCode and toString overrides.

  • The parameter type of == makes no meaningful difference: == (dynamic other), == (Object other) and == (Object? other) are within 4.1% of each other at N=4000, which is within the run-to-run noise of a single compile.
  • Overriding == costs 1.82s (1.2×) at N=4000 (== (dynamic other) at 12.3s vs. no == override at 10.4s). The biggest difference is in Enqueue (456ms, 25% of it), mostly resolution.dynamicUse (379ms). Scaling goes from N1.50 to N1.45.
  • Adding a hashCode override to a toString override costs 1.07s (1.1×) at N=4000 (no == override at 10.4s vs. toString only at 9.36s). The biggest difference is in kernel loader (203ms, 19% of it). Scaling goes from N1.57 to N1.50.
  • Adding a toString override to a hashCode override costs 598ms (1.1×) at N=4000 (no == override at 10.4s vs. hashCode only at 9.84s). The biggest difference is in SSA optimizer (134ms, 22% of it). Scaling goes from N1.54 to N1.50.
  • Reading the shared field val inside toString costs 7.43s (4.9×) at N=4000 (toString only at 9.36s vs. toString only, no field read at 1.93s). The biggest difference is in Enqueue (5.21s, 70% of it), mostly resolution.dynamicUse (5.19s). Scaling goes from N0.70 to N1.57.
  • A toString override that does not read any field costs 464ms (1.3×) at N=4000 (toString only, no field read at 1.93s vs. no overrides at 1.47s). The biggest difference is in SSA optimizer (90ms, 19% of it). Scaling goes from N0.66 to N0.70.
  • Every class declaring a field with the same name (vs. unique names) costs 6.96s (2.3×) at N=4000 (== (dynamic other) at 12.3s vs. == (dynamic other), unique field names at 5.29s). The biggest difference is in Enqueue (5.49s, 79% of it), mostly resolution.dynamicUse (5.48s). Scaling goes from N0.97 to N1.45.
  • Declaring val on every subclass (vs. once on the base class) costs 7.71s (2.7×) at N=4000 (== (dynamic other) at 12.3s vs. == (dynamic other), field on base class at 4.54s). The biggest difference is in Enqueue (5.50s, 71% of it), mostly resolution.dynamicUse (5.48s). Scaling goes from N0.90 to N1.45.
  • All N inserts in one giant main (vs. helpers of 100 statements) costs 5.58s (1.8×) at N=4000 (== (dynamic other) at 12.3s vs. == (dynamic other), main split up at 6.68s). The biggest difference is in Enqueue (5.40s, 97% of it), mostly resolution.dynamicUse (5.42s). Scaling goes from N1.08 to N1.45.
  • A giant main once field names are unique makes little difference at N=4000 (== (dynamic other), unique field names at 5.29s vs. unique field names + main split up at 5.30s). Scaling goes from N0.94 to N0.97.
  • All classes in one library (vs. a library per class, same public field name) saves 1.93s (1.2×) at N=4000 (== (dynamic other) at 12.3s vs. == (dynamic other), library per class at 14.2s). The biggest difference is in kernel loader (1.16s, 60% of it). Scaling goes from N1.31 to N1.45.
  • A public field name shared across libraries (vs. a private _val per library) costs 6.00s (1.7×) at N=4000 (== (dynamic other), library per class at 14.2s vs. == (dynamic other), library per class, private _val at 8.19s). The biggest difference is in Enqueue (5.04s, 84% of it), mostly resolution.dynamicUse (5.01s). Scaling goes from N1.05 to N1.31.

Comparing variants: Frugal-style structs

Each N adds one struct shaped like Frugal’s generated Dart (six fields whose names id, name, description, count, tags and child are shared by every struct; child is the previous struct), in its own library, plus a service client calling through FMethod. So N=1000 is 2000 classes. The variants apply the generator changes recommended in research/frugal-dart-codegen.md. These stop at N=1000 because they are much slower to compile.

  • Generated internals going through the shared public getters, isSetX() and validate() (vs. private fields and _validate()) costs 9.59s (1.4×) at N=1000 (Frugal-style, as generated today at 32.9s vs. Frugal-style, internals use private fields and _validate() at 23.4s). The biggest difference is in SSA builder (4.44s, 46% of it). Scaling goes from N1.08 to N1.20.
  • FMethod calling Function.apply on a tear-off (vs. a typed closure) makes little difference at N=1000 (Frugal-style, as generated today at 32.9s vs. Frugal-style, FMethod without Function.apply at 32.9s). Scaling goes from N1.21 to N1.20.
  • static final descriptors, implicit dynamic return types and a new DeepCollectionEquality per call (vs. const, explicit types and a shared instance) costs 1.79s (1.1×) at N=1000 (Frugal-style, as generated today at 32.9s vs. Frugal-style, const descriptors and explicit return types at 31.2s). The biggest difference is in Enqueue (484ms, 27% of it), mostly resolution.dynamicUse (416ms). Scaling goes from N1.20 to N1.20.
  • Generating getFieldValue, setFieldValue, isSet, clone and toString (vs. a lean mode without them) costs 10.5s (1.5×) at N=1000 (Frugal-style, as generated today at 32.9s vs. Frugal-style, no getFieldValue/setFieldValue/isSet/clone/toString at 22.4s). The biggest difference is in SSA builder (3.79s, 36% of it). Scaling goes from N1.20 to N1.20.
  • Inline list loops in read/write (vs. shared runtime helpers) makes little difference at N=1000 (Frugal-style, as generated today at 32.9s vs. Frugal-style, shared list read/write helpers at 31.9s). Scaling goes from N1.21 to N1.20.
  • Frugal output as generated today (vs. all recommended changes together) costs 17.0s (2.1×) at N=1000 (Frugal-style, as generated today at 32.9s vs. Frugal-style, all of the above at 15.9s). The biggest difference is in SSA builder (6.42s, 38% of it). Scaling goes from N1.07 to N1.20.

Breakdown for == (dynamic other)

  • Compile time went from 381ms at N=1 to 12.3s at N=4000, 32× slower for 4000× more classes. From N=1000 up it scales as roughly N1.45 (superlinear).
  • Most of the extra time comes from Enqueue (+5.74s, 48% of the increase), SSA builder (+1.98s, 17% of the increase) and SSA optimizer (+1.26s, 11% of the increase).
  • Fastest-growing phases that take at least 5% of the time at N=4000: Enqueue > resolution.dynamicUse (N2.44, 45% of the time), Enqueue (N2.27, 47% of the time) and SSA builder (N1.49, 16% of the time). These grow faster than the total, so they will dominate even more at larger N.
  • Between N=100 and N=4000, Enqueue grew from 6.2% to 47% of compile time, while kernel loader fell from 35% to 6.1%.
  • The amount of work dart2js reports grows at most as N0.96 (about 41 inferred types per class), but time grows as N1.45. The cost per element is rising with program size, which points at non-linear behavior inside the phases above rather than just more code to compile.
  • Outside the compiler itself (VM startup, make), each compile costs a roughly fixed 142ms of wall-clock time on average.

  • Compile time went from 321ms at N=1 to 11.8s at N=4000, 37× slower for 4000× more classes. From N=1000 up it scales as roughly N1.40 (superlinear).
  • Most of the extra time comes from Enqueue (+5.36s, 47% of the increase), SSA builder (+1.94s, 17% of the increase) and SSA optimizer (+1.25s, 11% of the increase).
  • Fastest-growing phases that take at least 5% of the time at N=4000: Enqueue > resolution.dynamicUse (N2.21, 43% of the time), Enqueue (N2.08, 46% of the time) and SSA builder (N1.49, 17% of the time). These grow faster than the total, so they will dominate even more at larger N.

  • The amount of work dart2js reports grows at most as N0.96 (about 41 inferred types per class), but time grows as N1.40. The cost per element is rising with program size, which points at non-linear behavior inside the phases above rather than just more code to compile.

  • Compile time went from 320ms at N=1 to 9.84s at N=4000, 31× slower for 4000× more classes. From N=1000 up it scales as roughly N1.54 (superlinear).

Breakdown for Frugal-style, all of the above

  • Compile time went from 420ms at N=1 to 15.9s at N=1000, 38× slower for 1000× more classes. From N=250 up it scales as roughly N1.07 (about linear).
  • Most of the extra time comes from SSA builder (+2.65s, 17% of the increase), Enqueue (+2.51s, 16% of the increase) and kernel loader (+2.15s, 14% of the increase).
  • Fastest-growing phases that take at least 5% of the time at N=1000: Enqueue > resolution.dynamicUse (N2.03, 12% of the time), Enqueue (N1.72, 16% of the time) and SSA builder (N1.16, 17% of the time). These grow faster than the total, so they will dominate even more at larger N.
  • Between N=100 and N=1000, Enqueue grew from 5.1% to 16% of compile time, while kernel loader fell from 22% to 14%.
  • The amount of work dart2js reports grows as roughly N0.96 (about 639 inferred types per class), in line with compile time. The slowdown is mostly explained by there being more code, not by a per-item cost that grows.
  • Outside the compiler itself (VM startup, make), each compile costs a roughly fixed 90ms of wall-clock time on average.

Where the time goes

Top-level dart2js phases stacked, so the top edge is the total compile time.

On log-log axes a phase growing as Nk is a straight line with slope k. Lines steeper than the total are taking a growing share of compile time.
